item.title: 30+ AI Art Styles: Visual Examples and Prompt Ideas
item.description:
30+ AI Art Styles: Visual Examples and Prompt Ideas

See how different AI art styles change the same idea, with side-by-side examples and prompt variations created in Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni.
Kling AI
Aug 27, 2026
16 min read
1. What Are AI Art Styles?
2. Different AI Art Styles With Prompts and Examples
Traditional Painting and Drawing Styles
Anime, Comic, and Illustration Styles
Digital and 3D Styles
Graphic and Design Styles
Portrait, Photography, and Cinematic Styles
Futuristic, Fantasy, and Experimental Styles
3. What You Can Do With Kling AI Art Generator
Tell More With a Single Frame
Carry the Story Across a Series
Catch the Details That Matter
Finish in 2K or 4K
4. How to Write AI Art Style Prompts
For Narrative and Realistic Scenes
For Cinematic Scenes
For Stylized Images
For a Series of Images
Keep the Wording Concrete
Change Only What Needs Fixing
5. FAQs
What Are the Different Styles of AI Art?
How Do You Write Anime Art Style Prompts for AI?
Can I Combine Two Art Styles in One AI Image Prompt?

AI art styles can be used in very different ways, from social posts and posters to character concepts and personal projects. A glossy 3D treatment might suit an Instagram post, watercolor can give a shop banner a softer finish, and anime can reshape the personality of a character idea. The difference often comes from a handful of choices: brushwork, outlines, light, color, and composition. Below, we use Kling AI Image Generator to explore 30+ AI art styles, with prompts you can tweak for your own ideas.

 

What Are AI Art Styles?

AI art styles are the visual directions that shape how a generated image looks and feels. A style can come from a traditional medium such as watercolor or charcoal, an art movement such as Impressionism or Art Deco, a digital format such as pixel art or 3D rendering, or a cinematic treatment built from camera language, lighting, color, and texture. The style does not replace the subject of a prompt; it tells the image model how to interpret and present that subject.

For creators, the useful distinction is between content and appearance. “A red fox reading beside a cabin window” describes content. “Soft watercolor washes, visible paper grain, cool dusk palette, gentle edge bleeding” describes appearance. When those two parts are clear, the result is easier to direct than a prompt that simply asks for something “artistic” or “beautiful.”

Different AI Art Styles With Prompts and Examples

With that distinction in mind, we’ve grouped 30+ styles into six groups and focused on the details that set each one apart. Within each group, the same base scene is reworked through image-to-image generation in Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni, making it easier to compare different art styles for AI side by side and see how linework, color, texture, lighting, and composition change.

Traditional Painting and Drawing Styles

Brush marks, paper grain, pencil lines, and charcoal smudges are part of the character here. We’ve picked seven traditional looks to show how the same scene can shift when the medium changes.

 

  • Watercolor: Color tends to feather at the edges, with the paper often showing through beneath lighter washes.
  • Gouache: More opaque than watercolor, gouache leans toward flatter color and stronger shapes while still looking painted.
  • Oil Painting: Layered strokes, deeper shadows, and richer highlights give the scene more weight and depth.
  • Colored Pencil: Fine lines and cross-hatching bring in detail without hiding the grain of the paper underneath.
  • Charcoal Sketch: Smudges, broken contours, and untouched areas of paper give charcoal its rough, sketchbook quality.
  • Ink Illustration: Black lines, hatching, and strong contrast carry most of the detail, with little need for color.
  • Impressionism: Edges become less precise as short brush marks, shifting color, and reflected light take over.

To see what each approach actually changes, we use the same rainy flower shop as our starting point. The subject stays put while the wording around the medium, marks, color, and surface changes. We then run each version through Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni and place the results side by side.

Paint It Your Way

Anime, Comic, and Illustration Styles

Linework, proportion, shading, and print texture carry most of the personality here. We’ve picked six illustrated directions to show how the same character scene can shift from polished anime to flatter graphic art or softer storybook imagery.

  • Japanese Anime: Crisp linework, cel-style shading, and expressive features keep the character visually clear and lively.
  • Manga-Inspired: Black ink, stronger shadows, and sharper angles move the portrait closer to a printed manga panel.
  • 2D Chibi: An oversized head, compact body, and simplified features reshape the character into a cuter, exaggerated proportion.
  • Vintage Comic: Heavy outlines, halftone dots, and flatter color bring in the punch of older print comics.
  • Children’s Picture Book: Rounded forms and a gentler painted finish soften the portrait into something closer to a storybook page.
  • Gongbi Painting: Fine linework and carefully layered color bring out small details, with a more precise and polished finish than looser brush styles.

The same red-backdrop portrait carries through every version, with the pose, double-bun hairstyle, and outfit left unchanged so the differences between anime, manga, chibi, comic, and other illustrated looks are easier to spot.

Reimagine Your Character

Digital and 3D Styles

Digital and 3D treatments shift the focus toward form, material, and depth. The four directions here take the same setup from smooth and dimensional to faceted, pixelated, or molded.

  • 3D Render: Materials, reflections, and shadows help the objects read as solid forms rather than flat drawings.
  • Low-Poly 3D: Smooth curves give way to visible facets, making the scene feel more geometric and deliberately simplified.
  • Pixel Art: The grid becomes part of the image, with hard edges and stepped color replacing smooth transitions.
  • 3D Clay: Rounded shapes and a molded surface give everyday objects a softer, hand-shaped quality.

The city stays recognizable throughout, from the waterfront and high-rises to the aircraft overhead. What changes is how each treatment handles the buildings, depth, and overall surface of the scene.

 

Give It a Digital Twist

Graphic and Design Styles

Graphic design relies on how elements are arranged as much as on what appears in the frame. Geometry, ornament, color blocks, and empty space can push the same subject toward very different design traditions.

  • Art Deco: Symmetry, stepped forms, and decorative geometry bring a sleek, architectural order to the composition.
  • Art Nouveau: Flowing curves, botanical motifs, and ornate borders replace harder structure with something more organic.
  • Bauhaus: Primary colors, simple geometry, and asymmetrical grids keep the design pared back and purposeful.
  • Minimalism: Less is doing more here, with fewer objects and wider areas of open space drawing attention to the main subject.
  • Vintage Propaganda Poster: Bold silhouettes, a tight color range, and strong contrast give the poster a more forceful, direct presence.

For this comparison, the observatory remains the centerpiece while everything around it is reworked through a different design language. One version leans into symmetry, another into curves or open space, making the shift easy to read without changing the subject itself.

Turn It Into a Poster

Portrait, Photography, and Cinematic Styles

This group leans on camera language rather than drawn marks. We’ve picked six directions to show how the same portrait scene can move from natural photography to editorial styling, film-inspired color, or a more dramatic movie frame.

  • Photorealistic Portrait: Skin, light, depth, and surface detail stay close to what you would expect from a natural camera shot.
  • High-Fashion Editorial: Styling, pose, and stronger lighting make the portrait feel more deliberate and magazine-driven.
  • Movie Still: Framing, shadow, and color hint at a larger story beyond the frame.
  • Film Noir: Deep contrast, moody light, and darker tonal treatment pull the scene toward classic noir.
  • Kodak Portra 400 Film Look: Softer contrast and gentle color give the portrait a familiar film-stock warmth.
  • Ricoh Nostalgia: Muted tones and a slightly nostalgic finish make the scene feel quieter and more reflective.

We use the same café portrait to compare different photographic looks, changing the light, framing, tone, and finish while keeping the subject familiar.

Restyle Your Portrait

Futuristic, Fantasy, and Experimental Styles

These styles loosen the rules of the real world. A desert railway city can borrow from an older vision of the future, sink into neon, slip into dream logic, or grow into something far more imagined.

  • Retro-Futurism: Chrome, rounded machinery, analog controls, and mid-century forms picture the future through an old-school lens.
  • Cyberpunk: Neon signs, exposed cables, worn surfaces, and crowded technology pack the city with grit and energy.
  • Synthwave: Hot pink and violet skies, glowing horizons, and geometric suns give the landscape a bold retro-digital edge.
  • Surrealism: Familiar buildings remain, but scale, placement, and physical logic no longer behave as expected.
  • Fantasy Concept Art: Towering structures, distant haze, and invented landmarks make the city seem like one small part of a much larger imagined world.

The railway station gives the set a common thread, but little else has to stay fixed. Across the five versions, the city shifts in era, color, scale, and even in what counts as physically possible.

These types of art styles for AI prompts range from traditional painting and illustration to 3D, photography, graphic design, and more experimental directions. Which one fits best depends on what you want the image to communicate and which details matter most.

Take It Beyond Reality

What You Can Do With Kling AI Art Generator

Art direction is only part of the job. The way a shot is framed, how a character carries into the next scene, and whether small details survive the process can matter just as much. Kling AI art generator brings those pieces together in one image workflow.

Tell More With a Single Frame

A simple character image can be the starting point for an entire story. With image-to-image AI in IMAGE 3.0 Omni, a simple base image and a text prompt can move the character into a crowded subway car, set the action, framing, light, and focus, and turn the setup into a film-like moment with tension and story.

Carry the Story Across a Series

Some ideas need more than one frame. Image Series Mode can build a connected set from one or several reference images, carrying characters, settings, and the broader direction from shot to shot. That opens up room for storyboards, character sequences, campaign sets, and social content without rebuilding the setup every time.

Catch the Details That Matter

Loose strands of hair, fabric weave, skin texture, reflections, and subtle shifts in light can change how convincing a result feels. IMAGE 3.0 Omni is designed to pick up finer elements while keeping key subjects, tone, and atmosphere in step across related work. That matters when refining a portrait, trying several art directions, or working through a longer set.

Finish in 2K or 4K

A quick concept and a full-size poster do not need the same level of resolution. IMAGE 3.0 Omni supports direct 2K and 4K output, leaving more room for fine texture and smoother color transitions. The higher-resolution option is suited to posters, brand graphics, product visuals, concept boards, previsualization, and other work intended for larger displays.

How to Write AI Art Style Prompts

From there, different kinds of images call for different details. A list of art styles for AI prompts can point you in the right direction, but narrative scenes, cinematic shots, stylized work, and image series each need a slightly different approach. Below, we break down what matters most for each one.

For Narrative and Realistic Scenes

When the picture needs to capture a moment, describe what the subject is doing and where it is happening.

A useful structure is:

Style + subject + action + setting + details + light + mood

For example:

Film grain. Blonde curly-haired woman in a navy top, head tilted back, eyes closed, laughing. Open desert with dry brush and a modified silver bus. Natural skin and cotton texture. Harsh sunlight, double-rainbow lens flare, strong rim light. Subject placed mid-right against a blue sky and sandy yellow ground. Shallow depth of field, face in focus. Free-spirited atmosphere.

The action gives the picture its story, while the setting, light, and small surface details make the moment more specific.

For Cinematic Scenes

Film-inspired shots usually need tighter control over framing and light.

Try:

Style + subject + setting + light + composition + angle + focus + color + mood

For example:

Real cinema look. Man in a dark suit, gray shirt, and glasses at an airport, giving an alert side glance. Posters and flight screens behind him. Mixed daylight and cool interior light. Medium shot at eye level, sharp focus on the face with soft background bokeh. Cool tones, light film grain, tense atmosphere.

Here, details such as medium shot, eye level, face focus, and cool light do more work than adding extra adjectives.

For Stylized Images

Illustration and character-led work can spend less space on camera terms and more on proportions, clothing, linework, texture, and surrounding details.

A useful structure is:

Art style + subject + pose or expression + clothing + setting + mood

For example:

2D anime style. Young girl with light-brown curls and wispy bangs, large sparkling eyes and soft blush. Forest-inspired Lolita dress with white lace, vine embroidery, puffy sleeves, lace socks, brown Mary Janes, pearl necklace, and flower clips. Holding a flower basket with a shy downward smile. Blurred petals in the foreground, warm wood interior behind her, soft daylight and creamy background blur. Gentle, playful atmosphere.

The same idea can be adapted for watercolor, chibi, vintage comic, pixel art, or other AI art styles by replacing the features that define the finish.

For a Series of Images

A single frame can vary freely. A sequence usually needs a few details to carry over.

Use references for anything that should remain recognizable:

Character reference + setting reference + action + continuity details

For a story sequence:

Use Ref 1 for Character A, Ref 2 for Character B, and Ref 3 for the setting. Character A confronts Character B as the two groups meet in the courtyard. Keep their faces, clothing, and surrounding architecture recognizable across the sequence.

For portraits, posters, product shots, or other non-narrative sets, references can instead hold the character, surroundings, composition, or overall art direction together.

Keep the Wording Concrete

Terms such as beautiful, professional, or stunning leave plenty open to interpretation. Specific details are usually more useful.

  • Instead of beautiful lighting, write late-afternoon sun hitting one side of the face.
  • Instead of rich texture, write thick brush marks around the highlights.
  • Instead of nice colors, write muted sage, cream, and dusty rose.

Faded tones, worn furniture, yellowed paper, low contrast, and warm evening light can all give the scene a more nostalgic feel.

Change Only What Needs Fixing

If the subject already works, leave it alone. If the setting feels right, keep it. Adjust the light, framing, color, texture, or art direction rather than rebuilding everything from scratch.

This is especially useful when testing different art styles on a familiar subject. Fewer changes make the differences between watercolor, anime, film noir, cyberpunk, and other directions much easier to spot.

FAQs

What Are the Different Styles of AI Art?

Many popular AI art styles draw from familiar art forms, including watercolor, oil painting, charcoal, anime, cel shading, vintage comics, Impressionism, Cubism, and Surrealism. Tools like Kling AI can read these cues in a prompt and translate them into color, linework, texture, and composition. Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni can also turn text into images and carry an idea into a related series.

How Do You Write Anime Art Style Prompts for AI?

For anime art prompts, describe the character first, including the hairstyle, outfit, expression, pose, and setting, then add a few traits that define the finish, such as clean outlines, cel shading, expressive eyes, or a soft color palette. An AI image generator like Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni can work with both written cues and reference images, helping keep the character and overall appearance recognizable across related images.

Can I Combine Two Art Styles in One AI Image Prompt?

Yes, you can mix two art styles in one AI image prompt. It usually works better when they are not competing for the same job. Anime can guide the character design, for instance, while watercolor handles the background, light, and color. Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni can work from both text and reference images, giving you room to combine the two without relying on style names alone.

Final Thoughts

AI art styles can set the direction, but the final result depends just as much on the subject, composition, light, color, and texture. Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni can read these cues from text and reference images, helping you shape the overall art direction and carry the same idea across a connected series. From there, that direction can extend into portraits, posters, storyboards, and other creative work.

Explore More AI Art Styles

This guide explores the best face swap AI tools for creating realistic photos and videos, from quick edits to character-driven storytelling. Learn how Kling IMAGE 3.0 and Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni use reference-based workflows to preserve facial details and character consistency across creative projects.

Best AI Face Swap Tools for Videos

From Precise Image Editing to Creative Visual Stories

Responsible Face Swapping

What Is the Best Face Swap AI ?
What Makes a Face Swap Look Realistic?
Is There a Free AI Face Swap?
Is AI face swapping legal?
The End

AI face swaps used to be mostly for fun on TikTok or Instagram, like putting your face into a movie clip just to see how it looks. These days, people are using them for much more, from testing character ideas and updating old footage to avoiding another round of reshoots or making social content faster. The best face swap AI should do more than paste one face onto another. It should keep the person looking like themselves as expressions, angles, lighting, and movement change. In this guide, we look at several popular options, what each one does well, where it can struggle, and which features actually matter, so you can find the right fit for your photos, videos, and workflow.

What is an AI face swap tool?

An AI face swap tool lets you replace one person’s face with another in a photo or video. Face swaps usually take two forms: photos and videos. They are commonly used for social media content, character testing, previsualization, video editing, marketing creative, and other visual projects.

Image Face Swap Tools

A photo face swap works with a single still image. The replacement needs to fit the original head angle, expression, and proportions while blending with the existing lighting, skin tone, texture, and composition. When these details are off, the new face can look like an added layer instead of a natural part of the image.

Video Face Swap Tools

Video face swaps are more challenging because the face has to adapt throughout the entire clip as the scene changes. A face that looks right in one frame may reveal problems when the person turns, speaks, changes expression, or moves through different lighting.

As the camera and subject move, the swapped face needs to follow those changes without flickering, unnatural movement, or noticeable shifts between frames.

How to Select the Best Face Swap AI Tool

Photo and video face swaps solve different problems, so the features you compare will depend on the type of content you want to create.

What to Look for in an Image Face Swap Tool

The main challenge in photo face swaps is whether the new face can be integrated into the original picture seamlessly.

What to Look for in a Video Face Swap Tool

With video, the challenge is not just getting one good frame. It is whether the face still works once the person starts moving.

One Standard That Applies to Both Images and Videos

No matter the format, image rights and responsible use matter. A face swap process should rely on authorized materials and avoid misleading content or using someone’s identity without permission.

Best AI Face Swap Tools for Videos and Images in 2026

Not all face swap tools are made for the same kind of project. Some are better for quick social edits and some give creators more control when a character needs to appear in new scenes, styles or different shots.

We looked at popular options, how well they fit, what they do well, and what to consider before you choose one.

Best AI Face Swap Tools for Images

Best AI Face Swap Tools for Videos

 

Kling AI is designed not only for replacing faces, but for creating consistent characters that can continue across images, videos, scenes, and stories.

What AI Face Swap Tool Should You Pick?

The right one will depend on what you want to make.

For a quick photo edit or social post, simple face swap apps may be enough. If you want to place the same character into different scenes, adjust the style, or build a longer visual sequence, reference-based workflows offer more flexibility.

For images, Kling IMAGE 3.0 is better suited to creative photo workflows where the character needs to appear in different visual settings. For video, Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni is designed for more involved projects where a character needs to carry through changing scenes, angles, and shots.

Try AI Face Swap

From Precise Image Editing to Creative Visual Stories

For photo face swaps and detailed image edits, Kling IMAGE 3.0 provides more control over the final image. With support for up to 10 reference images, it can understand key facial details, important visual elements, and overall style from multiple inputs.

This makes it easier to refine facial features, adjust specific details, and create new image versions while keeping the original look and feel. It is suitable for portrait edits, character adjustments, campaign visuals, and other projects where accuracy and detail matter.

Try Kling IMAGE 3.0 Now

 

For projects that go beyond a single image, Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni helps turn one character or concept into a wider range of visual scenes. It can bring ideas into different environments, styles, and compositions, making images feel more connected and story-driven.

Whether creating a character across different settings, developing a visual series, or exploring a new concept, IMAGE 3.0 Omni provides more room to build a complete visual direction.

Try Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni Now

Bring Characters Across Different Shots and Stories

Video face swaps require more than a good-looking single frame. A face that works in one moment still needs to feel right when the subject turns, changes expression, or moves through a different shot.

With Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni, you can go beyond a single reference image to fully capture every detail of your subject. By incorporating multiple views or character elements, you provide the AI with richer visual context to lock in key identity traits. This ensures your character remains effortlessly consistent across changing poses, camera motions, and scene transitions—making it ideal for dynamic, multi-shot video generation.

 

A finished face swap does not have to be the end of the process. With Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni, the edited clip can become the base for new ideas.

After the swap, you can:

  • Rework an existing clip: Keep the subject and performance, then change the setting, wardrobe, or other visual details with an AI video editor.
  • Try a different look: Restyle footage you already have instead of rebuilding the scene from scratch.
  • Continue into the next shot: A finished clip can become the starting point for an extended video sequence, so the idea can keep moving without resetting the whole setup.

Starting with a single portrait, an image-to-video workflow can bring the subject into motion and open the door to new scenes, actions, and visual styles. Combined with an AI video generator, face swapping can become part of a larger video creation process.

Think of it like keeping the actor while changing the set. A new scene does not always require starting from zero.

Try Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni Now

Responsible Face Swapping

A polished edit can travel far beyond the place you first post it, so it helps to think past the generation screen. Before sharing, ask three simple questions: Do I have the right to use the source material? Could viewers mistake the edit for something that really happened? Would the context change if the clip were used in an ad, campaign, or public post?

A few habits make that easier:

Keep track of where your photos, footage, and likeness references came from.

Review the final piece as a viewer would, especially if it could be mistaken for real footage.

Treat commercial work, client assets, and public-facing campaigns with extra care.

Store identifiable source files securely instead of leaving them scattered across devices or shared folders.

Check the platform’s current terms before publishing or reusing the result elsewhere.

A convincing edit is only half the job. Knowing where and how to use it matters just as much.

FAQs

What Is the Best Face Swap AI ?

The best face swap AI is the one that fits the kind of content you want to make. A quick photo edit may only need a simple app, but longer videos, multiple people, or recurring characters call for stronger continuity, cleaner results, and more room to adjust the final look.

What Makes a Face Swap Look Realistic?

A realistic face swap keeps the person recognizable while matching the original lighting, expression, and head angle. Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni can draw from multiple visual references and Character Elements, giving it more information about a person from different views. This helps facial details hold up better through turns, changing expressions, and camera movement, especially across video shots.

Is There a Free AI Face Swap?

Some face swap features may be available without a paid plan, but the limits can vary by model, video length, resolution, and the options you use. Since credits and pricing can change, it’s best to check the official Kling membership plan for the latest details before you start.

Is AI face swapping legal?

AI face swap videos can be legal in the United States, but consent and intended use matter. Using your own footage or material you have permission to edit is generally safer, while nonconsensual intimate deepfakes can violate the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act. Deceptive or unauthorized commercial uses may raise other legal issues, so get permission when a real person’s likeness is involved.

The End

The right AI face swap tool depends on the vision behind the project. For detailed image edits, Kling IMAGE 3.0 helps refine facial features, retain key traits, and adjust specific elements while keeping the original style intact. When a simple portrait needs to become something bigger, Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni opens up new possibilities by bringing characters into different scenes, styles, and visual narratives. For video, Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni takes that idea into motion, allowing the same character to move through changing angles, expressions, and shots. From a single portrait to a character that moves through different worlds, the right tool can turn a simple face swap into a story worth exploring.

6. Final Thoughts

From animated movies and comics to video games, brand mascots, and digital illustrations, cartoon art is everywhere. Behind every memorable cartoon character is a unique style shaped by colors, shapes, and visual choices. Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni makes it easier to experiment with different cartoon styles for AI, explore new looks for characters, and create scenes and stories based on your ideas.

What Are Cartoon Styles for AI?

Cartoon styles for AI describe how AI image generators can transform characters, scenes, and illustrations into different cartoon looks. They influence details such as line quality, colors, shapes, proportions, textures, and lighting, helping you decide how a character or scene should appear.

With AI cartoon styles, you can keep the same character while trying out new artistic looks. A portrait can take on a 3D animated look, an anime-inspired illustration, a comic-style design, or a hand-drawn feel. The character stays familiar, while changes in color, shape, and details give it a new personality and mood.

What Elements Shape AI Cartoon Styles?

A cartoon look is built from small choices that shape how a character feels on screen. By adjusting the way a subject is drawn, colored, or placed in a scene, you can achieve a new appearance without changing the core idea.

How AI Cartoon Styles Differ from Traditional Cartoon Art

Traditional cartoon artwork usually requires artists to draw each character, scene, and variation separately. With AI art generators, you can work from a text prompt or reference image and test several cartoon looks without redrawing the subject from scratch.

30+ Cartoon Styles for AI With Examples

The same character can feel completely different depending on the cartoon style you choose. From hand-drawn illustrations to 3D animated looks, different cartoon styles for AI bring their own approach to shapes, colors, and details. We’ve grouped 30+ popular styles into 8 categories, with comparisons and visual examples to show what makes each one unique.

Traditional 2D Animation Styles

Traditional 2D animation is generally based on hand-drawn artwork, using a sequence of drawings, key poses, and careful timing to create movement. With AI image generation, you can use text prompts or reference images to recreate hand-drawn linework, cel-style coloring, and the look of 2D animation from different eras.

 

Draw It in Classic 2D

2. Anime and Manga Styles

Anime and manga cover a wide range of looks, with linework, proportions, color, and pacing changing across eras and artists. Depending on the prompt or reference image, the same subject might appear as full-color anime, black-and-white manga, chibi, a ’90s animation look, or something softer and hand-drawn.

3. 3D and Stop-Motion-Inspired Styles

3D animation can give a scene more depth, volume, and a stronger sense of space. For AI-generated cartoons, the finish might be polished and cinematic, molded from clay, built from low-poly shapes, or made to resemble a collectible toy.

4. Comic and Graphic Art Styles

Comic and graphic art relies heavily on how a page is drawn and arranged. Panels break up the action, ink gives forms more weight, and color can pull attention to a face, gesture, or key moment. The result can range from a dense action panel to a spare newspaper strip or a bright pop-art print.

5. Digital and Vector-Style Cartoon

Digital cartoons can look sleek, flat, chunky, or deliberately rough around the edges. Vector pieces usually rely on smooth curves and sharp outlines. Flat drawings and stickers cut back on shading, while pixel art keeps the blocky grid visible and often works with a smaller color range.

6. Handcrafted Illustration Styles

Handcrafted illustration keeps the marks of the medium in view. Watercolor can bleed into the paper, pencil leaves uneven strokes, and cut paper shows its layers and edges. In AI-generated images, these details can give the result more of a painted, sketched, or handmade quality.

7. Retro and Nostalgic Styles

Retro cartoons often pick up details from earlier decades, whether that means faded print, old-school fashion, mid-century machinery, or the cel-colored look of ’90s animation.

8. Experimental and Mixed-Media Styles

AI-generated cartoons can mix digital rendering with collage, rough textures, and unexpected materials, making the image feel more layered and handmade.

Create Your Cartoon

Why Use Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni for AI Cartoon Styles?

Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni gives you more control when exploring different cartoon styles for AI. Start from a text prompt or reference image, then guide details such as composition, character appearance, lighting, and visual style to shape the result around your idea.

 

For projects that need more than one image, Image Series Mode can generate multiple related visuals while helping maintain recognizable subject details, style tone, and atmosphere across the series. This makes it useful for character concepts, storyboards, social content, and other projects where visual continuity matters. You can also generate images in native 2K or 4K resolution when your cartoon artwork needs finer details or higher-resolution output.

How to Create Cartoon Styles with Kling AI Prompts and References

Once you know the cartoon direction you want to explore, the next step is choosing the right way to create it. Below, we’ll look at three practical approaches with Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni: transforming a reference image, creating a cartoon from a text prompt, and generating a consistent series of related images.

1. Turn a Reference Image Into a Cartoon

If you already have a photo or illustration you like, image to image AI lets you use it as the starting point. Simply describe the cartoon treatment you want and build from there.

To keep the person recognizable, mention the details that should stay the same, such as the hairstyle, clothing, facial features, or overall silhouette.

2. Create from Text

No reference image? You can start with a written idea using text to image generation. Describe the subject, cartoon direction, defining traits, and setting so Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni has a clearer sense of what you want.

A simple structure to follow: Subject + Cartoon Direction + Defining Traits + Setting

3. Create Consistent Cartoon Image Series

When working on a series of cartoon images, small details can start to drift from one frame to the next. Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni’s new Image Series Mode lets you generate multiple related images while helping keep recognizable subject features and the overall visual direction aligned across the set. This makes it easier to create character variations, storyboards, social content, and other connected visuals without rebuilding the same creative setup for every image.

Create Cartoon Now

FAQs

What are different cartoon styles for AI?

There are plenty of different cartoon styles for AI, including classic 2D, anime, manga, 3D, watercolor, pixel art, chibi, low poly, collage, and retro-inspired looks. Some lean on bold outlines and flat color, while others use softer brushwork, visible texture, or more dimensional rendering. The right choice depends on whether you want something playful, graphic, handmade, nostalgic, or more polished.

What Are the Main Types of Cartoon Styles for AI?

There isn’t one fixed way to classify cartoon art. A practical approach is to group it by how the image is drawn or rendered, such as 2D animation, illustrated or handcrafted work, digital graphics, 3D treatments, retro aesthetics, and mixed media. From there, more specific directions like chibi, low poly, watercolor, or collage are easier to compare.

How do I choose a cartoon style for my photo?

Pick based on where the photo will be used and the feeling you want. 3D or vector art fits profile pictures and polished graphics, while chibi, sticker, and retro treatments suit lighter social posts. Comic, pop art, and mixed media make more sense when you want stronger contrast or a bolder finish. Comparing a few versions of the same photo is usually the fastest way to see which one feels right.

What is the difference between cartoon styles and AI art styles?

Cartoon styles mainly describe illustrated, animated, or comic-like results. AI art styles cover a wider field, from cartoons and photorealism to oil painting, impressionism, surrealism, and more. In practice, “cartoon style” usually refers to how a character or scene is drawn, while “AI art” can describe many other ways an image is rendered. Cartoon imagery is simply one area within that broader range.

Final Thoughts

Cartoon styles for AI can change how the same character, scene, or idea comes across, from classic 2D and anime to 3D, watercolor, retro, and mixed-media looks. Once you find a direction you like, Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni lets you work from text or reference images, refine the details that matter, and carry that look into new scenes or a connected image series. You can also use the AI image generator to keep building on the idea and see how far the same character or concept can go.

How do I swap a face in a picture?
Can I use multiple reference images for a face swap?
Why does my face swap look unnatural?
Is face swapping safe to use?
5. The End

Maybe you want to place your own face into portrait images with different outfits, hairstyles, or makeup, or see how the same person would look in a new style without changing the rest of the photo. Face swapping makes that much easier. In this guide, you’ll learn how to swap faces in pictures with Kling IMAGE 3.0 and avoid common problems that can throw off the result.

 

How to Face Swap Pictures With AI

Before you start, choose a reliable AI face swap tool. A good tool should do more than simply place one face onto another photo. With Kling IMAGE 3.0, you can work from a target image and one or more face references, while giving clear instructions about what should change and what should stay the same. Here’s how to face swap pictures with Kling AI in three steps.

Step 1: Choose and Upload Your Target Photo and Face Reference

Start with the photo you want to edit, then add a clear face reference. Choose one where the face is easy to see, with minimal obstruction, and try to keep the angle and expression close to the target photo.

With image-to-image AI, you can work from the original photo and use reference images to guide the face change. If one reference does not provide enough information, Kling IMAGE 3.0 supports up to 10 reference images, letting you add the same person from different angles and expressions. A front-facing photo can help define the overall facial structure, while side views can add details such as the profile, nose bridge, and jawline. References with different expressions can also help capture changes around the eyes, mouth, and overall look. Taken together, these views give the model a fuller picture of the person’s facial features and appearance, helping the face swap stay closer to the reference.

Step 2: Describe the Face Swap You Want

If you’re changing only the face, tell Kling IMAGE 3.0 which person to replace and note that the hairstyle, clothing, pose, lighting, and background should stay as they are. If a reference image contains more than one person, point out which face to use so the model picks the right one without changing the rest of the image.

Step 3: Generate Your Face Swap

Once the target photo, references, and instructions are ready, generate the image. Kling AI uses these inputs to create the face swap while helping preserve the original pose, lighting, and surrounding scene. You can export with Kling IMAGE 3.0 at up to 2K, or use Kling IMAGE 3.0 Omni for up to 4K when the final image needs more detail.

If you want to make a few more changes after the face swap, you can keep editing the image with Kling IMAGE 3.0, from adjusting the expression or hairstyle to changing the lighting and other details.

FAQs

How do I swap a face in a picture?

Here’s how to face swap a picture: upload the photo you want to edit along with a clear face reference, then tell the tool which face to replace. Generate the image, check how the face fits the original photo, and adjust the reference or prompt if something looks off. A similar angle and expression can make the match easier.

Can I use multiple reference images for a face swap?

Yes. If one photo does not show enough of the face, you can add other views of the same person. Different angles can provide details that are missing from a single reference, which is especially useful when the target face is turned or partly in profile. Kling IMAGE 3.0 supports multiple reference images for this kind of edit.

Why does my face swap look unnatural?

A face swap can look wrong when the reference and target are too different in angle, expression, or lighting. Hair, shadows, or a small face in the frame can also throw things off. Try a clearer reference, a closer angle, or another view of the same person. If other parts of the image change too, make the prompt clearer about what should stay untouched.

Is face swapping safe to use?

Face swapping can be used responsibly, but only when you have permission to use the person’s likeness and avoid deceptive, harmful, or misleading content. In the U.S., right of publicity laws can also affect how a person’s likeness is used, especially in commercial work. Face swaps can be used for memes, profile photos, personal projects, and other permitted creative work. For commercial use, confirm that you have the necessary likeness rights and comply with applicable terms.

The End

Whether you’re fixing one awkward face in a group photo or putting someone into a completely different scene, learning how to face swap comes down to a few basics: a clear reference, a workable angle, and a prompt that says what should stay unchanged. Kling IMAGE 3.0 gives you room to fine-tune the details, while IMAGE 3.0 Omni can take the same person into new scenes, storyboards, and connected shots.
